title: What If You Could Win Every Argument?

shots.line: Breakfast.
Your little sister points her spoon at you.
Broccoli is a fruit, she says.
She talks for 10 seconds.
You answer in two.
Broccoli is a flower.
You're about to eat a flower.
She stares. Then she eats it.
At school, your teacher says your essay is late.
You point at the clock.
It was early, by four minutes.
He checks. He sighs.
Full marks.
A man at the bus stop yells that buses never come on time.
You show him the timetable.
He reads it.
He apologizes to the timetable.
A lawyer in an expensive suit says you can't lock your bike here.
You smile.
You quote the sign, word for word.
He moves his car.
Three arguments, three wins.
Before lunch, you didn't raise your voice once. You barely even thought, and your cat still won't get off your keyboard.
Your name is Max, and your brain works differently.
A normal person speaks about 150 words a minute.
They hold about four ideas in mind at once.
You? You hold 40.
And when someone stops talking, they answer in roughly two tenths of a second. That's a blink.
You? You hear half a sentence and see the weak spot.
Every gap. Every trick. Every flaw.
You know which word they'll use next. Which fact they'll dodge.
It's like watching a chess game three moves early.
Then the perfect words arrive. Instantly. Like they were waiting for you.
Nobody gave you a manual. Just a normal Tuesday and a brain that woke up faster.
But there's a rule.
Your brain got faster at words. People did not get faster at changing.
You can win the argument, but you can't win the person.
They'll say you're right. Then they'll do exactly what they wanted.
So what if you could win every argument?
It starts small.
Your phone bill has a mystery fee.
The agent says it's policy.
You read her own policy back to her. Calmly.
She goes quiet.
The fee disappears.
Plus $40 saved.
Minus.
She sounds tired when she says goodbye.
Bedtime.
Your little sister Mia says she's not tired. Not even a little.
You list five reasons she is.
She yawns halfway through her own answer.
She goes to bed. No hug tonight.
Minus.
Your uncle swears he cooks better than your aunt.
You settle it at the table.
Nobody eats dessert.
A classmate swears the earth is flat. Just to test you.
You prove it's round in 60 seconds. With a lamp and a spoon.
He says fine. He still squints at the horizon.
Next week, Mia wants a puppy.
Your parents say no.
So you teach her. Five points.
Short ones. Calm ones.
Your mom listens. Your dad listens.
They say maybe.
Mia screams. In Mia language, that's a yes.
Mia draws a horse.
You spot the mistake instantly. Five legs.
You tell her. Kindly.
You're right. Mia's face crumbles.
She never shows you a drawing again.
Right. And somehow wrong.
Your teacher signs you up for debate club.
First round. Eight students. One after another.
You beat the first in 40 seconds.
The second in 30.
The eighth just shakes your hand.
The coach stares at you.
How… how did you do that?
You shrug. You really don't know.
You apply for a summer job.
12 minutes with the manager.
He asks why he should hire you. You tell him.
He asks when you can start. Today, he says, he's already sliding a uniform across the desk.
Then you open the internet.
Big mistake.
A comment war.
200 strangers.
You answer every single one in one evening.
Not one changes their mind. Of course not.
They just… stop replying. You still win. Technically.
Your neighbor argues about the fence.
You settle it in 90 seconds.
He stops waving at you.
Minus.
The principal wants to close the library on Saturdays.
You give her three reasons. She keeps it open.
Plus.
A boy in your class gets blamed for a missing laptop.
His story has a hole. You find it in 10 seconds. The time on the camera doesn't match.
He's cleared.
His mom hugs you in the hallway. Best wins so far.
On Saturday, a referee cancels Leo's goal.
Leo is furious.
You walk over. Calm.
You explain the offside law. Law 11.
The referee asks the linesman. Nods. Changes the call.
Leo grabs your shoulders. Dude.
That man has never changed a call in his life.
Leo's dad works nights at a warehouse.
His boss says the extra hours don't count.
You sit at their kitchen table with a notebook.
You add up every hour. Three pages.
His dad reads it twice.
Next month, his paycheck is bigger.
He tries to pay you in cake. You accept. Obviously.
A real lawyer, 40 years in court, volunteers to face you in a school mock trial.
12 minutes. Halfway through, she closes her folder.
Nobody has ever done that to her.
She asks to shake your hand.
Your landlord raises the rent.
Your mom stares at the letter.
You read the contract once. You find the clause.
You call him. Four minutes.
He cancels the raise.
Your mom cries. Good tears.
She hugs you so tight your ribs creak.
And you think, this is why you have it.
Then a famous host invites you on live TV.
Two million people watch.
He tries to corner you.
Three questions in, he's nodding.
Five questions in, he's agreeing. With you.
Your phone won't stop buzzing.
Even you have limits. Your coin gets stuck in a vending machine.
You give it your best argument. Out loud. For two minutes.
The machine does not care.
The catch?
You win every time.
And every time, the other person leaves a little smaller.
But where it gets really crazy is the city council.
Your street has no crosswalk. Kids cross anyway.
You speak for three minutes.
When you finish, the room is silent.
Then they vote. 11 to 0.
By spring, there's paint on the road. Bright yellow.
A little girl crosses it on her first day of school.
And you think, maybe this is what it's for.
Now the part nobody mentions.
Winning feels amazing. At first, dopamine cells fire hardest for surprises. For better than expected.
But you always expect to win. And you always do.
So nothing fires. No spark.
Just a quiet click. Like closing a drawer.
A win used to feel like a trophy. Now it feels like a receipt.
And your brain is paying for it. It's about 2 % of your body weight. But it burns about 20 % of your energy.
Yours burns more. You're starving by 10.
Headaches by noon.
At night, it gets worse. You lie awake.
Your brain replays arguments from hours ago. It finds a better answer to each.
At 2am, you're still winning fights that ended at lunch.
You start spotting flaws in everything.
A song. A joke. Your friend's story about his weekend.
You say so. Out loud. Once.
He never finishes the story.
Dr. Lee checks your scans.
Your brain is fine, Max. It's just running hot.
Eat. Sleep.
She pauses. And try losing sometimes.
Losing? Why?
Because a mind that never loses forgets how to listen.
Then at dinner, your dad says the garage needs cleaning.
You list six reasons it can wait.
He opens his mouth. Closes it.
Fine, Max. Fine.
Not you're right. Just fine.
Mia stops showing you her drawings.
She says you only look for mistakes.
At school, you stop raising your hand. Everyone already knows how it ends.
A teacher calls you the last word in every room. It doesn't sound like a compliment.
Nobody argues with you anymore. Your friends go quiet when you walk in.
Your mom stops asking what you think. Why would she?
You already won.
And something is coming. You can feel it.
There's one person you never argue against. Leo. Your best friend since you were six.
Left foot like a cannon.
His dad works night shifts so Leo can have real boots.
His dream fits in one sentence. Play for a real club.
And between you two, every fight ends the same way. The loser says, you win. I hate it.
The winner buys the churros.
Since you were eight, you've never used your power on Leo. Not once.
Because with Leo, you lose half the time.
And somehow, you love it.
He's the only person who tells you you're wrong. Then buys you food.
His dad comes to every match in work boots. Straight off a night shift. He falls asleep on the bench by half time.
Leo pretends not to notice. He always looks.
On your 10th birthday, Leo gave you a drawing. Two stick figures. One holds a trophy. One eats churros.
It's still on your wall.
Last spring, Leo missed a penalty.
In front of everyone.
Afterward, he sat alone on the grass.
You sat down next to him. You didn't say one clever thing.
You just stayed. An hour. Quiet.
Then he laughed. Churros? He asked. You nodded.
That's all. And it was the best conversation you've ever had.
Thursday, 9 p .m.
Your phone rings.
Leo is out of breath. Max, I met a scout.
Mr. Black. Big club.
He saw me play.
Your stomach drops. Slowly.
Don't tell my dad, Leo adds. It's a surprise.
You search for the club. Nothing. No website. No phone number. Nothing.
On the bus, you rehearse. 40 arguments. 10 answers each.
You've never prepared for anything in your life. You've never needed to.
Saturday, a hotel lobby.
Mr. Black wears a gray suit and a perfect smile.
A black car waits outside. The engine is running.
Leo sits across from him.
On the table lies an envelope. In his dad's handwriting. For Leo's future.
Four years of night shifts. All of it.
He opens a glossy folder. A club crest. A signature. A photo of a stadium.
You notice the crest is blurry. Pixelated at the edges.
Just a draft, says Mr. Black. Just a registration fee, son.
Then a flight tonight. A trial. A contract.
You listen for 10 seconds.
You find five holes. No club name. No website. Cash only. Today only. Tell no one.
You say all five in 30 seconds. Calm. Perfect.
A waiter freezes with a tray. A woman at the next table stops mid -sip.
Nobody in the lobby breathes.
Mr. Black opens his mouth. Nothing comes out.
He tries again. Nothing. Then he smiles.
Other scouts are watching, he tells Leo. If you wait, they'll go.
And somebody will try to talk you out of this. Probably someone jealous.
Leo turns to you. Slowly.
He said you'd say this. Leo whispers.
Your stomach turns to ice. He saw you coming.
Every argument you build is already inside his story.
You're right, Leo says, about everything.
You exhale.
Then Leo picks up the pen.
What? Why? You won!
Leo's eyes are wet. Because if you're right, it's gone.
His dream. His boots. His dad's face.
Leo doesn't need you to be right. He needs this to be true.

txt.s: HE NEEDS IT TO BE TRUE

shots.line: That's the rule. The one you forgot.
Leo's hand is 40 centimeters from the paper.
A nervous reach takes about two seconds. Two seconds is five words.
You have a thousand arguments. Not one fits.
30 centimeters. Mr. Black slides the page closer. 20.
The engine hums.
The flight leaves at 8.
Win the point or keep your best friend.
You let go. Your arguments fall away.
Every fact. Every number.
And you say five words.
You win. I hate it.
The lobby goes silent. A waiter lowers his tray.
Leo freezes. The pen stops. Three centimeters above the paper.
Because that's his line. The loser's line.
And you just said it. On purpose. To him.
How long has it been since you lost? Leo looks at you. Really looks.
Max? You never lose. For me? He whispers.
For you. You say.
Then your voice shakes. I'm scared. Not of him. Of losing you.
I don't have a better argument. I only know real scouts never ask for money first.
It's not a perfect sentence. It's not even a good one. But Leo hears every word.
The pen slips from his fingers. It rolls off the table.
Leo laughs through his tears. You really hate it. He says.
So much. You say.
Mr. Black stands. Smoothes his tie. Walks out.
The black car drives away. With an empty seat.
You could chase him. Ruin his name in an hour.
But then you'd just be another man who needs to win.
Instead, the hotel manager, who heard everything, picks up the phone and calls the police.
Leo calls his dad.
Ten minutes later, he arrives in his work boots.
He sees the envelope.
He sits down on the lobby floor. He doesn't say a word. He just holds his son.
A week later, the police find a drawer full of envelopes just like it.
Nobody in that lobby forgets what they saw.
That night, Leo's dad hugs you too. He smells like cardboard and coffee.
He doesn't say thank you.
He says, You're welcome at our table. Always.
Soon after, a real club offers Leo a free trial. Free.
At home, your mom says you're wrong about the garage.
You grin. Wrong? Explain.
And she does. For an hour, you lose every point.
And somewhere around the fifth, something lights up in your chest. Tiny. Warm. A spark.
You laugh right on time.
You can win a point. But a point isn't a person.
Saturday, Leo buys the churros.
That night, your phone buzzes.
Unknown number. One message. Impressive. I know someone who has never lost an argument either.
A pause. Then a second message.
Her name is Nova. She'd like to meet you.
So what's real?
Nobody wins every argument. Winning needs a judge. And the judge is always a person.
In 2011, Hugo Mercier and Dan Sperber argued that human reasoning evolved partly to persuade others and to judge their arguments.
But a brain that always wins? Pure fiction.
The cost is half real. Your brain really does burn about 20 % of your energy.
The starving part is exaggerated.
The dopamine part is real. In the 90s, Wolfram Schultz recorded dopamine cells in monkeys. They fire most when a reward is better than expected.
The speed is real, in part. In 2001, Nelson Cowan estimated that working memory holds about four items, not 40.
And a 2009 study of 10 languages found people reply in about 200 milliseconds. Fast enough that they start planning before the other person finishes.
Now, facts.
Scientists once worried that corrections make people dig in harder. The backfire effect. But a 2019 study by Thomas Wood and Ethan Porter found it's actually rare.
People can change their minds. Just slowly. And more easily when they feel heard.
And one lesson from this story is real. If someone says, pay today and tell no one, walk away.
So what really changes a mind? Being right or being heard?
What do you think? Tell us in the comments which argument you'd win first.
Tell us the worst argument you ever lost. We promise not to win it.
And tell us which superpower we should do next. And if your heart skipped when Max said those five words, hit like and subscribe for part two.
